query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a controlled fraction of tungsten carbide (WC) particles along with a minor Nb addition into a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix (via laser cladding) will promote an in situ reaction that forms uniformly distributed NbC and other carbide phases. These thermally stable carbides will act as self-adaptive, lubricious barriers during sliding, thereby maintaining a low coefficient of friction and low wear rate from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix with its standard microstructural and tribological characteristics.
generation.intervention: A single intervention comprising the addition of WC particles with a controlled minor amount of Nb to the CoCrFeNi matrix during the laser cladding process.
generation.conditions: Sliding experiments performed in a temperature-controlled chamber spanning from room temperature (approximately 25 °C) to 800 °C, under high contact pressures (e.g., ~0.9 GPa) in an ambient or inert atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: The in situ synthesized NbC and other carbide phases that result from the reaction between Nb and WC, ensuring a uniform distribution of hard, thermally stable, lubricious reinforcement in the alloy.
generation.mechanism: During processing, Nb reacts with WC to form NbC and aids in the dissolution and fine dispersion of WC-derived phases. These carbides resist deformation and delamination under high sliding stresses. Their presence reduces dislocation activity and minimizes stress concentration, thereby providing a lubricant-like effect that remains effective throughout large temperature variations.
generation.predicted_outcome: The composite HEA coating will show a significantly reduced average coefficient of friction and lower wear rates compared to the unmodified CoCrFeNi matrix across the full temperature range up to 800 °C, due to the thermally stable, self-lubricating carbide phases.
generation.baseline: The unmodified CoCrFeNi HEA matrix, when subjected to sliding, exhibits a higher coefficient of friction and increased wear, particularly at elevated temperatures, due to phase instabilities and the absence of reinforcing, lubricious phases.
generation.boundary: This intervention is anticipated to be effective in sliding applications where the contact pressures approximate 0.9 GPa, operating from room temperature to 800 °C in non-corrosive ambient or controlled atmospheres; environments with severe corrosives may require additional modifications.
generation.uncertainty: While the in situ formation of NbC and related carbides has been demonstrated in similar laser-cladded HEA coatings, its tribological performance and stability specifically at 800 °C remain to be validated. Additionally, the long-term effects under cyclic thermal loading may introduce complexities not accounted for in current studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of coatings on Q235B substrates using laser cladding: one set of CoCrFeNi HEA coatings modified with WC and a minor addition of Nb; and a control set of unmodified CoCrFeNi HEA coatings. Conduct ball-on-disk sliding tests where each sample is cycled through a controlled temperature ramp from room temperature up to 800 °C under identical contact pressures (≈0.9 GPa) and environmental conditions. Post-test, analyze the microstructure and phase composition to confirm the in situ formation of the carbide phases.
measurements: Average coefficient of friction across the temperature range
Surface morphology and wear debris analysis via SEM
Phase and microstructure characterization using XRD and TEM
Hardness profiles across the sliding track
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified coating does not show a statistically significant improvement (i.e., lower friction and reduced wear) compared to the control across the entire temperature range, or if the in situ synthesized NbC and related carbide phases are absent or not uniformly distributed after testing, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractQ235B is widely used in marine engineering materials; however, its wear resistance and corrosion resistance are poor. To improve wear and corrosion resistance, a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) composite coating was cladded using laser cladding (LC) technology. Different proportions of tungsten carbide (WC) and Nb elements were added to the CoCrFeNi HEA coating, and the microstructure, phase, hardness, wear, and corrosion resistance of three different composite coatings were analyzed. The results show that the in situ synthetic phase is composed of Face central cubic (FCC) (Cr3C2) and strengthening phases such as W, WC, and NbC. In the process of LC, Nb will react with WC in situ, which not only reduces the morphology of the CoCrFeNi HEA cladding coating changed by adding WC, but also generates NbC, which leads to the dissolution of WC particles and improves the uniformity of particle distribution of the coating. The hardness of the coating with Nb is increased by 1.40 times, the wear resistance is enhanced, and the peeling of the hard phase is reduced during wear. ## Abstract
AbstractHigh Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have garnered attention due to their remarkable tribological attributes. Predominantly, failure mechanisms in HEAs emanate from stress‐induced dislocations, culminating in crack propagation and film delamination. In this study, we report on the synthesis of 2D HEA of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 which facilitates shear‐induced energy dissipation at sliding interfaces. The ball‐on‐disk tribological investigations demonstrate unprecedentedly low average coefficients of friction (0.076) and wear rates (10−9 mm3 (N∙m)−1) under high contact pressures (0.936 GPa) within ambient conditions. Employing multi‐scale characterizations alongside molecular dynamic simulations, we elucidate that the presence of the HEA triggers tribocatalytic activity under high contact pressures emerging as a pivotal factor in extending lubricant lifespan during tribological tests. The resilient lubriciousness coupled with the facile spray coating methodology of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 in ambient environments paves the way for the development of a new class of solid lubricants based on 2D HEA.
